newsitem.title: GERMANY: Possible German BSE victim to undergo post-mortem.
newsitem.headline: Possible German BSE victim to undergo post-mortem.

text.p: German authorities received permission from relatives on Monday to carry out a post-mortem on a dead woman believed to be Germany's first victim of a condition related to mad cow disease.

The fact that the woman was only 41 suggests she may have been infected with a new, fast-acting strain of the brain-wasting Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease (CJD) which scientists have linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

The health ministry of Schleswig-Holstein state, where the woman died, said it had now persuaded her relatives to drop their objection to an autopsy -- the only way of confirming any presence of the disease.
The case has added to German consumers' worries about beef from Britain, which has had over 165,000 cases of BSE and where several people have died from what is believed to be BSE-related CJD.
It also coincides with the death of a fifth cow from BSE in Germany, announced last week.

Authorities fear the calf may have been the first BSE case born in Germany, albeit of a British cow, and so provide evidence of maternal transmission in addition to the well-known route via infected fodder.
The Bonn Institute for Molecular Diagnostics (IMD) is to test genetic material from the calf and its presumed father and sibling to establish its origin.
An IMD spokesman said on Monday that the genetic material had not yet arrived, and that it would take between two and 10 days to carry out the test.

Germany has already ordered the slaughter of over 5,000 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland, where BSE has also been widespread, as a precautionary measure to help restore consumer confidence in beef.
If the calf turns out not to be import but to have been born in Germany, the goverment has said 14,000 offspring of the British and Swiss cows must also be slaughtered.
